## 2. Full independent ordinary proof

For each n>=2 let k=n-1. Choose all k*n membership bits of S_i independently with probability 1/2 and write T_i=[n]\S_i. Only the zero pattern is random. Matrix rows are chosen afterwards as functions of the whole pattern; they are not claimed independent random field entries. Define E_n to be existence over F2 of an (n-1)-by-n matrix obeying the prescribed zeros and having all maximal minors nonsingular. We prove P(E_n) -> 1.

### Independent representatives: all fields and all finite family sizes

Let V_1,...,V_m be subspaces of a vector space over an arbitrary field. There exist independent representatives v_i in V_i if and only if dim(sum_{i in I} V_i)>=|I| for every subset I of [m]. This includes m=0, zero spaces, and infinite-dimensional ambient spaces. Necessity follows from the independent subfamily in each sum.

For sufficiency induct on m. The empty family works. For m=1 the singleton inequality supplies a nonzero vector. For m>1 suppose a nonempty proper I is tight: U=sum_I V_i has dimension |I|. The inequalities restricted to I and induction give independent representatives of size |I|, hence a basis of U. For each complementary index j pass to the image of V_j in the quotient by U. For every J in the complement, its sum of images has dimension dim((U+sum_J V_j)/U)>=|J|: if the numerator has finite dimension this follows by subtracting dim U=|I| from the original inequality on I union J; if it has infinite dimension, quotient by finite-dimensional U is still infinite-dimensional. Induction gives independent quotient representatives, and arbitrary lifts in their respective V_j together with the basis of U are independent (first project any linear relation to the quotient, then use the basis). Both families are strictly smaller than m.

If no nonempty proper subset is tight, choose any nonzero v_m in V_m and put L=span(v_m). For every nonempty J subset [m-1], its sum has dimension at least |J|+1 (or infinite), since J is proper. Quotienting by L loses at most one dimension, so its image sum has dimension at least |J|. The empty-set inequality is automatic. Induct in the quotient and lift. A relation among the lifts and v_m projects to zero, forcing all lift coefficients zero, and then the coefficient of v_m is zero. This completes the induction. No union-of-subspaces argument that could fail over a finite field was used.

### Support spaces, their dimensions, and the deterministic sufficient criterion

Let W={x in F2^n: sum_j x_j=0}; dim W=n-1, since the coordinate-sum functional is nonzero. For T subset [n] let V(T)={x in W: supp(x) subset T}. If T is empty its dimension is zero; if T is nonempty its dimension is |T|-1. For a chosen root r in T, the vectors e_a+e_r with a in T\{r} form a basis: coordinates away from r prove independence, and the zero-sum condition determines the root coordinate. Equivalently V(T) is spanned by all pair vectors e_a+e_b with distinct a,b in T. This covers singletons (empty basis) and all parities of |T|; the all-ones vector need not lie in W when n is odd.

For a nonempty row set I, build the graph on U=union_{i in I}T_i whose edges join pairs contained in some T_i. The sum of the V(T_i) is exactly the span of its edge vectors. More generally its dimension is |U|-r, where r is the number of connected components, counting isolated vertices. To prove this, every edge vector has even sum on each component. Within each component, summing edges along a path produces e_a+e_b, since internal coordinates occur twice in F2. A root in each component therefore supplies all zero-sum vectors on that component, with |component|-1 independent generators. Components have disjoint supports, so dimensions add. Empty U gives dimension zero. This also gives the exact representative criterion dim(sum_I V(T_i))>=|I| without any pairwise-intersection assumption.

For our convenient sufficient event impose:
(A) |union_{i in I}T_i|>=|I|+1 for every nonempty I subset [n-1];
(B) T_i intersects T_j for every distinct pair of rows.
Singletons in (A) ensure |T_i|>=2. For a singleton I the clique is connected. For larger I, the cliques on its T_i are connected and pairwise intersect by (B), so their union graph is connected on U. Thus dim(sum_I V(T_i))=|U|-1>=|I|. The representative lemma produces n-1 independent rows v_i in V(T_i), a basis of W. Membership in V(T_i) ensures every prescribed zero.

For each omitted column j, the coordinate projection pi_j:W -> F2^{[n]\{j}} is injective: a vector in its kernel is supported on {j}, and its coordinate sum zero forces its remaining coordinate to be zero. Domain and codomain both have dimension n-1, so it is an isomorphism. Hence the images under pi_j of the same row basis are independent for every j. Those are precisely all n choices of n-1 columns; every maximal square submatrix is invertible simultaneously. There is no fresh choice of rows for each minor. This proves E_n whenever (A) and (B) hold.

### Symbolic probability bound over every obstruction

For distinct rows i,j, each coordinate is absent from their intersection with probability 3/4, independently across coordinates. Consequently P(T_i intersect T_j is empty)=(3/4)^n and P(B fails)<=binom(n-1,2)(3/4)^n.

If (A) fails for some I of t rows, 1<=t<=n-1, their union has at most t columns. Enlarge that union to a t-element column set C. All t rows avoid all n-t columns outside C. The t(n-t) distinct membership bits specifying this avoidance are independent and each has probability 1/2. A union bound over row choices and column choices gives

P(A fails) <= sum_{t=1}^{n-1} binom(n-1,t) binom(n,t) 2^{-t(n-t)}.

This counts all obstructions, including t=1 and t=n-1; overcounting patterns is harmless. Set m=min(t,n-t)>=1. If t<=n/2, each binomial factor is at most n^t=n^m. If t>n/2, symmetry gives binom(n,t)=binom(n,m)<=n^m and binom(n-1,t)=binom(n-1,m-1)<=n^{m-1}<=n^m. Also t(n-t)=m(n-m)>=mn/2. Each summand is therefore at most a_n^m with a_n=n^2*2^{-n/2}. For sufficiently large n, 0<a_n<1, so a_n^m<=a_n. There are n-1 summands, whence

P(A fails)<=n^3*2^{-n/2} ->0.

The limit follows, for example, from log(n^3*2^{-n/2})=3 log n-(n/2)log 2 -> -infinity, since log n/n ->0. The pair-intersection error tends to zero by the same argument. Thus

P(E_n)>=1-n^3*2^{-n/2}-binom(n-1,2)(3/4)^n ->1.

The displayed bound is an eventual bound; for small n it need not be informative, and no finite tests are claimed. No independence between obstruction events, between (A) and (B), or among chosen rows is assumed.

### Negation for every absolute positive c

Fix any real c>0. Then c*n^c>2 for all sufficiently large n; equivalently choose n>(2/c)^(1/c). On E_n, a field of size exactly two realizes the required pattern. Therefore the event that every realizing field has size at least c*binom(n,n-1)^c=c*n^c is contained in E_n's complement for all such n. Its probability tends to zero, not one. The same argument applies if the conjecture is phrased about an arbitrary realizing pair (F,A), since we exhibit a violating pair on E_n. A lower-bound constant chosen separately for each n or each pattern would not be absolute; our conclusion does not depend on making that illicit choice.
